tool.name: MTBSBurnSeverity

summary.para:
View online help files: https://www.jennessent.com/data-tools/mtbs-burn-severity.html
Finds fires mapped by Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity (MTBS), a program of the U.S. Geological Survey and the USDA Forest Service, by name, year and place, and writes their perimeters. For each fire it can fetch the six-class burn severity raster, with every class named, and it can ask the Burn Severity Portal to email a link to the fire's data bundle, which holds the continuous dNBR and RdNBR. MTBS maps every fire of at least 1,000 acres in the western United States and 500 acres in the east, on all ownerships, since 1984. United States and its territories only. Works at every license level.

tool.usage:
What MTBS maps. MTBS compares a satellite image taken before a fire with one taken after it. From each image it computes the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR), which contrasts near-infrared light, which healthy vegetation reflects strongly, with shortwave-infrared light, which char and bare soil reflect strongly. The difference, pre-fire NBR minus post-fire NBR, is dNBR: the larger it is, the more the surface changed. An analyst then looks at each fire's dNBR and sets the thresholds that divide it into classes: unburned to low, low, moderate and high severity, increased greenness, and a mask for cells that could not be assessed.
The classes are set fire by fire. Because the thresholds are an analyst's judgment for each fire, "moderate" in one fire is not the same amount of change as "moderate" in another. MTBS says so itself: the classes are subjective, and their ecological meaning varies by region. The thresholds chosen for each fire are in the low_t, moderate_t and high_t fields of the perimeters. To compare fires on one scale, use the continuous dNBR or RdNBR of the data bundles.
What it measures. MTBS burn severity is the change seen from above in vegetation and soil together, a year or so after the fire for an extended assessment or within weeks for an initial one (the assessment field says which). It is not a measure of tree mortality, which RAVG estimates, nor of the condition of the soil, which BAER maps.
United States only. This is a program of the United States Government. It maps fires in the United States and its territories, and nowhere else.
Finding fires. Give any of a fire name, a range of years, a study area and the programs' fire IDs; a fire must match all that you give. The study area only selects fires: every fire whose perimeter touches it is written whole, including the parts outside it. Nothing is clipped.
The classified rasters are copies. The rasters this tool fetches come from public image services, which hold copies of the program's national mosaics in the Web Mercator coordinate system. They are right for looking and for overlay. Their cells are not 30 meters on the ground, so do not count cells to measure area. Each raster's attribute table names every class (Class_Name) and gives its true area (Hectares, Acres) and its share of the fire (Percent). Cells the program could not assess, such as cloud, are named as a mask class and left out of the percentages. The original cells, in the fire's own projection, are in the fire's data bundle.
Which fires have a raster. The image services carry MTBS's yearly national mosaics. A fire mapped after its year's mosaic was made is not in it yet, and the tool says which fires those are. Their rasters are in their data bundles.
Data bundles come by email. A fire's data bundle holds what the image services do not: the continuous indices, in the fire's own projection with true 30-meter cells, and the rasters of fires too recent to be in the national mosaics. The Burn Severity Portal does not hand bundles to a program. Give an email address and this tool asks the portal for the bundles of every fire it found, in one request of up to 500 fires. Nothing is downloaded by the tool. The portal sends an email with a link, usually within minutes; you download the zip file yourself (the link works for 30 days), and then run the Load Burn Severity Bundle tool on it.
The internet. The tool reads the fire catalog of the Burn Severity Portal and the image services of the U.S. Geological Survey and the USDA Forest Service. If the fire catalog cannot be reached, the tool stops with a message that names it, and writes nothing. If a raster service cannot be reached, the perimeters are still written and the rasters are reported as not fetched.

param.name: fire_name
param.displayname: Fire name (all or part of it; several separated by semicolons)

dialogReference.para: All or part of a fire's name, in capitals or not: museum finds MUSEUM. Several names can be given, separated by semicolons, and a fire matching any of them is found. Many fires share a name, so give years or a study area as well. Empty for any name.
Give at least a fire name, a year, a study area or a fire ID.
The first year of ignition to include. MTBS begins with the fires of 1984. Empty for no limit.
The last year of ignition to include. Empty for no limit. For one year, give the same year in both boxes.

A year later than the current one is accepted, so 9999 means "through the latest fires". The tool then asks for fires through the current year, and its messages name the years that were not available.

A polygon layer or feature class. Selected polygons are used when there is a selection, and a definition query is honored. Every fire whose perimeter touches a polygon is found and written whole: the study area selects fires and does not clip them.

param.name: extent
param.displayname: Or a rectangle as the study area

dialogReference.para: A rectangle, in any coordinate system. Every fire whose perimeter touches it is found and written whole. Give a study area layer or a rectangle, not both.

param.name: fire_ids
param.displayname: Fire IDs (the programs' event identifiers, separated by semicolons)

dialogReference.para: The identifiers the programs give fires, such as AZ3525811164320190721 (the state, the latitude and longitude of the fire's center, and the ignition date). They are in the fire_id field of this tool's output, and the same fire has the same identifier in MTBS, RAVG and BAER. Use them to ask for exactly the fires you mean.

An identifier stands for every assessment of the fire. A fire can have more than one: an initial and an extended assessment, for example. To ask for one of them only, add a colon and that assessment's map ID (the map_id field of this tool's output), as in AZ3525811164320190721:10016328.

param.name: out_perimeters
param.displayname: Output fire perimeters (in a file geodatabase)

dialogReference.para: The polygon feature class to create, directly inside a file geodatabase, with one perimeter for each fire found and the fire's name, identifier, ignition date, type, acres and the thresholds its analyst set. An existing feature class of that name is replaced.

param.name: products
param.displayname: Classified rasters to fetch for each fire

dialogReference.para: Thematic burn severity (6 classes): MTBS's burn severity raster, with the classes Unburned to Low, Low, Moderate, High, Increased Greenness and Non-Processing Area Mask. It is cut to the fire's perimeter, and its attribute table names each class and gives its area. Uncheck it to write the perimeters alone.

The raster comes from a public image service, which holds a copy of MTBS's yearly national mosaics in the Web Mercator coordinate system: right for looking and for overlay, not for counting cells to measure area. A fire mapped after its year's mosaic was made is not in it yet. The fire's data bundle holds the original.

param.name: raster_workspace
param.displayname: Folder or file geodatabase for the rasters (empty: the geodatabase of the perimeters)

dialogReference.para: Where the classified rasters are written: a folder (GeoTIFF files) or a file geodatabase. Left empty, they go into the geodatabase of the output perimeters. Each raster is named for its program, fire, year and product, and a raster of the same name is replaced. Used only when a classified raster is chosen.

param.name: bundle_email
param.displayname: Email address for a request of the fires' data bundles (empty: no request)

dialogReference.para: An email address. When one is given, the tool asks the Burn Severity Portal to prepare the data bundles of every fire it found and to send a download link to this address. Nothing is downloaded by the tool: you open the email, download the zip file yourself, and run the Load Burn Severity Bundle tool on it. Empty for no request.

A bundle holds the fire's continuous indices, and its rasters in their own projection with their true cells. The portal takes at most 500 fires in one request. The address is sent to the portal and is not kept anywhere by this tool.

param.name: bundle_images
param.displayname: Include the pre-fire and post-fire images in the bundles

dialogReference.para: Checked, the bundle request also asks for the two satellite images each assessment was made from: the reflectance image taken before the fire and the one taken after it. They make the zip file much larger. Unchecked, the bundle holds the perimeter, the classified rasters and the continuous indices only. Used only when an email address is given.

The coordinate system the portal writes the bundle's rasters in. UTM (the default) is the zone of each fire, with true 30-meter cells, and suits work on one fire or one region. Albers is the single equal-area projection of the national mosaics, and suits work on fires spread across the country, because every fire is then on the same grid. Used only when an email address is given.
The number of fires that matched.
The classified rasters that were fetched.

scriptExample.title: MTBS Burn Severity example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: The perimeter and the six-class severity raster of the 2019 Museum Fire.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path # products options: 'Thematic burn severity (6 classes)'; products="" writes the perimeters alone # bundle_projection options: "UTM", "Albers" arcpy.jenness.MTBSBurnSeverity( fire_name="museum", year_from=2019, year_to=2019, out_perimeters=r"D:\data\fire.gdb\Museum_MTBS")

scriptExample.title: Every fire that touched a study area, with a request for the data bundles
scriptExample.para: All MTBS fires since 2000 whose perimeter touches a study area; perimeters only, and a request for the bundles by email.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path arcpy.jenness.MTBSBurnSeverity( year_from=2000, study_area=r"D:\data\fire.gdb\Study_Area", out_perimeters=r"D:\data\fire.gdb\MTBS_fires", products="", bundle_email="you@example.org")
